title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A Session with Students at Clemson University - Jan 27, 2021
summary: Speaking to students at his alma mater during the GameStop frenzy, Pabrai describes 2020 as his second-biggest year of learning: Nick Sleep's letters and Thomas Phelps's '100 to 1 in the Stock Market' pushed him from a buy-at-50-cents-sell-at-a-dollar treadmill toward owning great compounders with an entrepreneur's never-sell mindset. He explains why auction-driven markets overshoot, why shorting is a dumb asymmetric bet, why micro trumps macro, and walks through the Turkish warehouse investment (Reysas) bought at about $3 per square foot in 2019, along with his views on ESG, Bitcoin and market bubbles.

ideas.idea: 2020 was his second-biggest year of learning after 1994-95, because Nick Sleep's partnership letters and Thomas Phelps's '100 to 1 in the Stock Market' caused him to make significant changes to how he invests.
ideas.detail: Sleep ran a fund from 2001 to 2014 and his 13 years of letters are 'like the Dead Sea Scrolls'; read them oldest to newest. Phelps's 1972 book is 48 years old but timeless.

ideas.idea: Nick Sleep's question: if you owned Walmart in 1970 or 1980, what facts caused you to sell, and if you owned Kmart, what caused you to keep it?
ideas.detail: The Walton family has held Walmart since its 1970 IPO but almost no public investor held it even 20 years. Kmart was cheap on many metrics but in decline; Walmart looked expensive but was going from strength to strength.

ideas.idea: Buying dollar bills for 30-50 cents and selling near a dollar turned every $1 in Pabrai Funds into about $14 after fees over 21 years, but it is an inefficient treadmill compared with holding great businesses with long runways.
ideas.detail: A really good business will periodically look optically overvalued, maybe for a long time, and that should not by itself prompt a sale. The shift makes life easier, improves returns and cuts taxes.

ideas.idea: 'The best investors weren't investors at all; they were entrepreneurs who never sold' (Nick Sleep): think of yourself as the founder or owning family and ignore valuation as long as the moat is widening.
ideas.detail: The exception is egregious cases: a family owning GameStop right now should have sold a while ago. He has gradually begun shifting his portfolio to this mindset.

ideas.idea: Auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot: a random NYSE stock shows at least a 2-to-1 range between its yearly low and high while an apartment building near Clemson would be quoted at nearly the same price all year.
ideas.detail: Intelligent buyer facing intelligent seller yields rational prices; faceless auction pricing does not. Ben Graham: markets are voting machines short term and weighing machines long term. Without these distortions he could not make a living.

ideas.idea: Shorting is a very dumb activity: maximum gain is a double and maximum loss is infinite, so he has never shorted a stock and will go to his grave without doing so.
ideas.detail: He finds many things overvalued but has no ability to predict when or how overvaluation corrects; nothing prevents an overvalued stock from becoming more overvalued. Shorting heavily shorted stocks is playing with fire; an index or basket would be safer.

ideas.idea: The GameStop squeeze is unprecedented: a Reddit crowd that does not know each other is not illegal collusion but has broken market mechanisms, and the SEC is torn about the right response.
ideas.detail: GameStop's short thesis was justifiable given the secular shift from physical stores to downloads. The stock was at $303 during the talk, with online chatter aiming for $1,000 to wipe out hedge funds; one argument is to let the dumb hedge funds face the music.

ideas.idea: In January 2021 there are bubbles in SPACs, heavily shorted stocks and 10-15 Robinhood names including Tesla, but beyond those it is not clear the broader market is overvalued if rates stay low.
ideas.detail: GameStop has gone beyond a bubble to a mega bubble; Tesla is clearly in bubble territory in his view. The rest of the market seems richly valued but justifiable under low interest rates.

ideas.idea: Separate capitalism from doing good: you cannot optimize two variables, so focus investing on returns and create impact through philanthropy.
ideas.detail: He personally would not invest in tobacco and is not eager on casinos, sports betting or lotteries, but has invested in a liquor company and in carbon-heavy car companies, and would not argue much with others who draw different lines.

ideas.idea: Micro trumps macro: with 80% of the portfolio in six or seven positions, what matters is how those businesses perform, not who is president, which party controls Congress, or what the market does in 12 months.
ideas.detail: Buying a McDonald's in Clemson, you would look at its past cash flows and local demographics, nothing else. He has no idea what markets will do next year and does not care.

ideas.idea: In July 2019 Turkey's largest warehouse operator could be bought for about $40 million, under $3.50 per square foot for 12 million square feet leased 99% long-term to blue-chip tenants, against a liquidation value of $50-60 a foot.
ideas.detail: With about $17 a foot of debt, $3 of equity per foot would return about $33 in liquidation, 11x. Tenants include Amazon, Alibaba, Carrefour and IKEA; multinational leases are in euros with 2-3% escalators, Turkish leases inflation-indexed. He spent an afternoon visiting all the warehouses to rule out fraud and now owns one-third of the company, his largest percentage ownership ever.

ideas.idea: The Turkish lira fell 40% after he invested, yet the position is up six or seven times in dollars because prime warehouses have a global value regardless of whether the local currency is seashells, dollars or lira.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Currency instability, poor leadership and mass foreign exit were the macro backdrop in 2019, and none of it mattered. The exceptional father-son capital allocators have since done value-adding things he never had on his radar; he has no plans to sell.

ideas.idea: He would not hold Bitcoin: money is a medium of exchange valued by what we ascribe to it, and a Bitcoin worth $5 million defies logic, though 99% of the world he does not need to understand.
ideas.detail: He cites people losing hundreds of millions in Bitcoin to forgotten passwords and a UK hard drive with $280 million in a landfill (the owner offered $70 million to dig). He does not need to go long or short.

ideas.idea: Nick Sleep's model: when you find exceptional businesses with high returns on equity, long runways, great managers and deep moats, go all in, ideally find them small, then set it and forget it.
ideas.detail: In 2013 Sleep ran about $3 billion with 40% ($1.2 billion) in Amazon and 90% across Amazon, Costco and Berkshire, defying UK regulators. He compounded about 20% a year for 14 years, returned capital in 2014 with Amazon at $300 (now over $3,300), kept his own stake, and has since outperformed almost any manager while working perhaps 100 hours a year.

ideas.idea: He no longer does precise intrinsic-value calculations; he owns 4 million of Reysas's 12 million square feet through his funds and intends to keep the business for a long time rather than sell when it reaches full price.
ideas.detail: Before 2020 he viewed the Turkish investment as a temporary undervaluation to exit after a good run; now the mindset is ownership of a well-managed business.

ideas.idea: Repositioning the portfolio toward great compounders is like turning an aircraft carrier and will take a few years, after which the job is monitoring; his job has always been reading and thinking as a 'gentleman of leisure'.
ideas.detail: New positions were started in 2020 but the fund is 'pregnant with a bunch of positions' that must play out before the carrier is positioned correctly.
